Restaurant co-owner dumps water on protesters in Little Rock

Cruz protesters doused with water outside Cache restaurant

A small group of protesters picketing Ted Cruz outside a downtown Little Rock restaurant Tuesday night were doused with water by the business' head chef and owner.

According to a Little Rock Police Department report, James Bozeman told officers he and friends were protesting outside Cache, 425 President Clinton Ave., while Cruz and Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson were inside.

"Bozeman advised during their peaceful protest someone inside the restaurant, on the balcony, poured a pitcher of water onto" one of the protesters, police wrote in the report.

The report noted that the four protesters were unclear about who poured the water.

Arkansas Democrat-Gazette associate features editor Emily Van Zandt, who happened to be in the restaurant at the time with a group of reporters from the newspaper, said Cache executive chef and owner Payne Harding dumped the water from a champagne bucket while wearing his chef jacket bearing his name.

Harding issued a statement Wednesday apologizing "to James Ryan Bozeman along with every individual affected by the events that took place last evening."

"This was a heat of the moment action driven by frustration; these actions were in no way shape or form politically motivated," Harding said. "Customers were having difficulty entering and exiting the restaurant and I thought it was causing a problem for my business. I did not know who the protesters were or what they were protesting. It was as simple as a poor decision that, given the opportunity to make again, I would obviously think about the consequences before I acted. Cache is, and will always be, an establishment that welcomes everyone. There is no excuse for my actions, and I sincerely apologize."

Jennifer Pierce, who was also in the group of picketers, said earlier that they were "speaking with lawyers on legal action."

Officer Richard Hilgeman said police didn't make an arrest and planned no further action. He said the protesters could request prosecutors issue a warrant, though he noted that the report didn't even list a suspect.

"All we've got is that report," Hilgeman said. "It's up to the prosecutor if they can press any charges. I wouldn't expect there to be warrants issued."

I think it's because the internet wasn't really a place to speak your mind. It was such a place once, but it was quietly turned on its head by massive spying. A few years ago, much of the public was blissfully unaware that they were being watched, then came Assange and Snowden and others...

Suddenly everyone knew that the people they called "conspiratards" were right all along. Suddenly everyone was saying:

"Oh, yeah -- I always knew. Ignore my prior statements and eyerolls about 'conspiracy nuts.' I knew all along, and so I am very smart."

The public re-wrote their own memories about how oblivious they all were, and in the process the public was engaging in cognitive dissonance that still haunts many people deep in the back of their brains.

Deep down many of them still have glimpses of doubt:

"I have a vague recollection - I think maybe I used to mock these guys .. no .. no that would mean I was fooled. Surely I am smart, so I knew it all along."

So we have a huge segment of the global population thinking these thoughts, and digging in their heels. It is causing people to expect no privacy at all. This leads to them demanding no privacy, and an accepting that this is all just "the way it is."

So the public now has some idea that the internet just wasn't ever made for free expression, and they fall neatly into line. They want an opportunity to show how uber-smart they are about (the lack of) privacy. So when you see a massive doxxing threat going on at AshleyMadison.com, people just point their fingers and mock the victims now:

"Hurr hurr! You were dum! I would never be that dum! I know there's no privacy, and I've come to peace with that fact. See how smart I am?"

This was all triggered when the Assange/Snowden revelations became public. At the moment, the public stood at a crossroads with two choices:

1) Rail against what is happening and demand privacy. Engage tools that help them to take control of their own privacy. Express disgust at their governments and oust the people who have done these evil deeds.

or

2) Look for people who are being burned at the stake because their privacy was violated, and join in the mob, laughing as the poor saps are burned alive - smugly self- assured that "I'm far to clever to have such as fate!"

A startling number of people chose "2)." They'd rather mock the idea of privacy than fight for it. To keep this sort of decision consistent, one often feels the need to become "pro-censorship" as well.
